meta.title: Just Enough Software Architecture: A Risk-Driven Approach
meta.author: George Fairbanks

parts.title: Understanding Software Architecture: A Practical Guide

sentences: **Software architecture** is a crucial aspect of **software development**, especially as systems grow in **complexity** and **scale**.
As Alan Kay noted, a good "**point of view**" can boost understanding significantly.
This book describes **"just enough" architecture**, a **risk-driven** approach centered on optimizing the balance of solving design challenges without overcomplicating the system.
By effectively using **abstractions**, such as **components** and **connectors**, developers can handle complexity while ensuring **maintainability** and **scalability**.
The book encourages **practical application** of software architecture within hours of reading, providing both theory and real-world insights.
**Software Architecture** plays a crucial role in designing systems by impacting system *qualities* like **performance**, **security**, and **modifiability**.
It is vital to understand architecture as it acts as the system's **skeleton**, influencing its *quality attributes* and imposing necessary constraints.
By considering architecture as mostly orthogonal to **functionality**, you can better match system requirements and attributes.

**Architecture-indifferent**, **architecture-focused**, and **architecture hoisting** are three levels of architectural engagement, highlighting the attention you should pay to your system's architectural needs depending on complexity, domain knowledge, and risk.

parts.title: Integrating and Risks with COTS Components

sentences: We start by **integrating two new COTS** components: Cross Platform AV and NextGenVideo, for our **Home Media Player**.
This involves exploring their **interface compatibility** and identifying any potential **architectural mismatches**.
NextGenVideo, although high-performance, **crashes with imperfect files**, posing a **reliability risk**.
To address these risks, we design a solution that uses **adapters** for each port of NextGenVideo to fit within our existing architecture, as visualized in a **component assembly**.
We validate this design by **prototyping**, referring to functionality **scenarios** for guidance.
Alongside, we ensure **reliable playback** by implementing measures to **detect and isolate crashes** of NextGenVideo.
The canonical model structure in software architecture uses **three primary models**: the **domain model**, the **design model**, and the **code model**.
These models range from abstract to concrete, allowing for organized representation and connection through **designation and refinement** relationships.
This structure ensures coherence across different abstraction levels and uses **views** to select and focus on specific elements or relationships, making management of complex systems easier.

parts.title: Relationship of Domain, Design, and Code Models

paragraphs.heading: Relationship of Domain, Design, and Code Models
sentences: This chunk emphasizes the importance of organizing the **domain**, **design**, and **code models** as separate entities, each representing different aspects of the system.

The **domain model** reflects real-world truths (e.g., contact networks in a phone system), while the **design model** is about the system architecture (e.g., how your system represents and manipulates those contacts).
This separation helps in **clarifying responsibilities** and **focusing design efforts**, allowing each model to be fully developed without distraction from other concerns.
**Design elements** like components, connectors, and ports are crucial for understanding interactions and functioning within the system.
**Quality attributes** such as security, performance, and usability are highlighted as essential considerations in the design process.
Overall, there is a focus on **consistency** and **cohesion** across models, ensuring that **views** generated from these models are clear, practical, and focused on required details.

parts.title: Model-Code Gap and Expressing Design Intent

sentences: The **Code Model** chapter explores the relationship between architecture models and source code.
It highlights the differences in **vocabulary**, **abstraction levels**, and **expressions** of design intent between models and code.
**Architecture models** typically use terms such as "components" and "connectors," which may encompass multiple elements in code like classes and methods.
Moreover, they include high-level **design principles** and **intentions**, such as protocols and constraints, that may not be directly represented in code.
The **model-code gap** refers to this difference, where the more **intensional** (rule-based) aspects of models are not easily expressed in code, which is typically more **extensional** (enumerated).
In designing **dynamic architectures**, it's crucial to keep things simple by restricting operations to basic node changes like adding or removing them.
This helps in understanding potential **configurations** and constraints.
However, be wary of **anti-patterns** like **Buried Treasure**, where responsibilities are hinted at but not followed through, possibly misleading **readers**.
Ensure method names reflect their actions, preventing surprises.
To help manage architecture, **component frameworks** like **OSGi** and **.NET** can be used.
These frameworks provide runtime management and have components/modules managed via **manifest files**.
While beneficial, these frameworks can conflict with some **architecturally-evident coding patterns**.
They often excel at runtime module management but may require adjustment in code structure for **Java EE** or similar systems.

**Connectors** in software architecture are elements that connect components, serving as a communication channel between them and can be swapped without affecting the clients if they maintain the same **interface**.
This flexibility is often lost when translating models into **code** as developers implement connectors directly, making **client dependencies** specific to the connector implementation.
**Selecting connectors** is a choice influenced by efficiency, complexity, and system requirements like cross-machine communication or emergent properties.
Giving connectors **first-class status** lets you reassess or change their implementation without impacting users, facilitating adaptation to evolving **system integrations** or requirements.

parts.title: Key Model Traits and Working with Views

sentences: A **good model** has traits like **accuracy**, precision, and consistency in **detail level** *(not all parts more detailed than others)*.
It also **promotes understanding** by **limiting details** and focusing **attention**.
Models should be suited to their **purpose**: a favorite view can mislead if it doesn’t fit the problem, and a single diagram for all details can be **confusing**.
Use **views** to **focus concerns** (like performance or security) but remain aware of **problems** caused by extreme **narrow focus** or **interactions between views**.
Avoid **"favorite view”** and **"one diagram to rule them all"** anti-patterns.
Gather views to build a whole model, using **scenarios** to **connect views**, and **activity specs** to tie together actions.

parts.title: Using Legends and Typographic Elements in Diagrams for Clarity

paragraphs.heading: Improving Diagram Quality
sentences: Adding **detailed legends** to your diagrams is helpful because it forces you to carefully consider the **notations** you use.
It also guides the reader effectively, providing insight into the **architecture** being illustrated.
Clear and precise legends can prevent your diagrams from becoming ambiguous, where readers may misinterpret elements like **connectors** and their directional **arrowheads**.
For instance, using **multiple arrowheads** can be confusing if not explained, as they can imply different interactions like **data requests or responses**.
To avoid misinterpretation, consider using distinctive **typographic elements** and provide a **detailed legend** to represent various aspects of **connectors** and **ports**.
This ensures diagrams are clear about the intended direction of interaction while leaving more complex properties to be described elsewhere, such as in detailed text or legends.
